title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 89
paragraphs: Hearing this, Cyrus was beyond measure pleased, because he thought that Croesus gave good counsel. He praised him highly and enjoined the spearmen of his guard to carry out what Croesus had advised. After that, he spoke to Croesus thus: “Croesus, since you are prepared, like the king you are, to do good deeds and speak good words, therefore ask me for a gift, whatever you wish to be given you forthwith.” And Croesus said: “Master, you will most of all do me a pleasure if you permit me to send to the god of the Greeks, whom I honored most of all the gods, these fetters, and to ask him whether it is reckoned right by him to deceive those who do well by him.” Then Cyrus asked him what accusation he was making against the god, that he should make such a request; and Croesus repeated to him everything that had been in his mind, and the answers of the Oracles, and especially the votive offerings, and how he had been incited by the prophecy to march against the Persians; and thus speaking, he came back again to the request that he might be permitted to make this reproach against the god. And Cyrus laughed and said: “Not only this shall you obtain from me, Croesus, but also whatever you may at any time desire of me.” Hearing this, Croesus sent certain of the Lydians to Delphi, enjoining them to lay the fetters upon the threshold of the temple and to ask the god whether he felt no shame at having incited Croesus by his prophecies to march against the Persians, persuading him that he would bring an end to the empire of Cyrus—seeing that these fetters were the first-fruits of the spoil he had won from it—at the same time displaying the fetters. This they were to ask, and moreover whether it was considered right by the gods of the Greeks to practice ingratitude.
